home.title: Three sources. One question: do they agree?
home.lede: SahamatiCheck reads an Android app's privacy policy, its Play data-safety declaration and its APK, then shows you, sentence by sentence, where they agree and where they appear inconsistent.
home.demoCaption: Chai Wallet is a fabricated demo app.

how.title: Read
how.body: The policy is split into sentences and turned into claim tuples: who does what with which data, and when.

how.title: Map
how.body: Data-safety rows, Android permissions and SDK packages are mapped onto the same ontology of data types.

how.title: Compare
how.body: Claims are compared only where one data type contains the other. Siblings never count as overlap.

how.title: Show
how.body: Each finding carries both quotes, a confidence and a tier. Agreement is shown first.

principles.title: No score, ever
principles.body: A grade is a verdict. Reports show tier counts, coverage and vagueness instead.

principles.title: Precision over recall
principles.body: Findings below a calibrated threshold stay hidden from public reports.

principles.title: Silence is not denial
principles.body: Things no source mentions sit in their own section and are never counted as conflicts.

principles.title: APKs never from Play
principles.body: APKs come from the AndroZoo research corpus or from a developer's own upload.

ontology.title: Ontology explorer
ontology.lede: Every comparison runs on this ontology. Two claims overlap only when one data type contains the other; siblings never overlap.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.lede: How SahamatiCheck turns three documents into evidence, and why it chooses precision over recall.

sections.title: The claim tuple
body: Every source is reduced to claim tuples: an actor, an action, a data type, an optional condition, and a polarity of affirm, deny or vague.

Policy sentences are read by a rule-based extractor that handles negation scope and exception clauses. A language-model fallback is used only for hard sentences, and every such call is logged for reproducibility.

sections.title: One ontology for three sources
body: Policy phrases, Play data-safety categories, Android permissions and SDK packages are all mapped onto one versioned ontology of data types, actors and purposes.
Two claims are compared only when one data type is an ancestor of the other. Siblings never overlap, so 'email' is never compared with 'phone number'.

sections.title: Four classes, three tiers
body: Internal contradictions and declaration mismatches compare two written claims and are tier strong.
Behavioural mismatches compare a written denial with evidence in the APK and are tier indicative, because a requested permission is not proof of use.
Disclosure gaps are APK evidence that no written source mentions. They are tier not mentioned and sit in their own section.

sections.title: Confidence and thresholds
body: Confidence is the class weight times the weaker side's confidence, times a specificity penalty for broad claims, times a penalty when negation scope was resolved heuristically.
Each class has a threshold set from precision-recall curves on a hand-annotated gold set. Findings below it are stored but never shown publicly.

sections.title: Data sourcing
body: Play listings are fetched only for user-requested apps and the fixed corpus, at one request every two seconds. APKs come only from the AndroZoo research corpus or from a developer's own self-check upload, never from Play.
The extension reads only the page the user is already viewing, and sends policy text only after the user asks.

sections.title: Limits
body: This is static analysis. It cannot see what an app does at run time, and a permission in the manifest may never be used.
Evaluation figures (inter-annotator agreement, precision-recall curves and failure rates) will be published here once the gold set is frozen.

methodology.formula: confidence = w_class × min(c_a, c_b) × s_spec × s_neg

rights.title: Your rights under the DPDP Act, 2023
rights.lede: A plain-language guide to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 for people in India. Not legal advice; check the commencement status of the DPDP Rules before relying on any provision.
rights.rightsTitle: Your rights as a Data Principal

items.title: Consent you can withdraw
items.body: Consent must be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, and you can withdraw it as easily as you gave it.

items.title: Access to information
items.body: You can ask a Data Fiduciary for a summary of your personal data being processed, the processing activities, and the identities of others it has shared your data with.

items.title: Correction and erasure
items.body: You can ask for your personal data to be corrected, completed, updated or erased.

items.title: Grievance redressal
items.body: You can raise a grievance with the Data Fiduciary, which must respond within the prescribed period. After that, you can approach the Data Protection Board of India.

items.title: Nominate someone
items.body: You can nominate another person to exercise your rights in case of death or incapacity.

rights.duties: Section 15 asks Data Principals not to file false or frivolous grievances and not to impersonate others. Keep requests factual.
rights.letterIntro: Send this to the grievance officer or contact named in the app's privacy policy. Keep a copy and the date.
rights.letter:
To the Grievance Officer,

I am a user of the app {app}. Under Section 11 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, I request a summary of the personal data about me that you process, the processing activities, and the identities of the Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom it has been shared.

I also note that your privacy policy and your Play data-safety section appear to describe the handling of {dataType} differently. Please clarify which description is accurate.

Please respond within the period prescribed under the Act.

about.title: About SahamatiCheck
about.lede: Sahamati means consent. Consent is only meaningful when what an app says, declares and does line up.
body: SahamatiCheck is an open-source B.Tech main project. It compares three sources for an Android app: the privacy policy, the Play data-safety declaration, and the APK's permissions and SDKs.
It ships as a Chrome extension and this website, both backed by one API. The clients only display results; all analysis lives in the backend.
Reports are user-initiated, unlisted and not indexed. Demos use fabricated apps only. The public audit shows aggregates only.
dispute: Developers can dispute any finding. Verify ownership through your Play contact email domain, or by placing a token on your policy page or under /.well-known/.
We acknowledge within 72 hours and hide the disputed finding while it is under review.
We then either fix the ruleset, with the change logged, or attach your response to the finding.
A public dispute log shows counts only.
about.emailHint: Use an address on your Play contact email domain if you can.

limitation.title: What this evidence cannot show
limitation.permission_only: Based on a permission only. A permission shows the app can do something, not that it does.
limitation.sdk_presence_only: Based on a library found in the app. Its presence does not show how the app uses it.
limitation.runtime_not_observed: We did not watch the app run, so we cannot say what it actually sends.
limitation.confidence_below_confirm_threshold: Our confidence is below the level we need to call this a confirmed difference.
limitation.generic: This result has a limit on what the evidence can show.
limitation.not_mentioned_only: This is a gap in what the policy and the safety section mention. Silence is not a denial.
limitation.conditional_denial: The statement depends on a condition, which we cannot check from the app alone.
limitation.broad_affirmation: One source is broader than the other, so they may not describe the same thing.
limitation.low_claim_confidence: We read one of these statements with low confidence.
limitation.tier_not_strong: This difference rests on the app's code, not on two written statements.
limitation.evidence_strength_insufficient: The evidence on one side is too weak to confirm a difference.
limitation.excluded_affirm_actor_is_exempt: The recipient may be a service provider, which the policy treats differently.
limitation.no_registry_rule: No check in this version covers this kind of difference, so it is shown for review only.
limitation.below_class_threshold: Our confidence is below the level we show publicly. Only you can see this.

reason.runtime_evidence_unavailable: Needs watching the app while it runs. This version only analyses the app statically.
reason.test_account_unavailable: Needs a test account to try the feature. None was available.
reason.apk_unavailable: The app package (APK) was not available, so checks that read the code did not run.
reason.apk_unparseable: The app package could not be read.
reason.apk_partial_coverage: The app package could only be partly read (its code is obfuscated), so a missing library or permission cannot be ruled out.
reason.policy_unavailable: The privacy policy could not be fetched or read.
reason.data_safety_unavailable: The Play data-safety section was not available.
reason.not_enabled_in_this_version: This check is not turned on in this version.
reason.missing_source_false_pass_prevented: A needed source was missing, so we did not report this as fine.
reason.generic: This check could not be completed.

rulesNotEvaluated.title: Rules not evaluated
rulesNotEvaluated.intro: These checks could not run with the evidence available. “Couldn't check” is never a pass: it means nothing can be said either way.
rulesNotEvaluated.none: Every enabled rule ran with usable sources.

indicators.intro: These are not differences between sources. They are things the app can do, shown so you can decide whether they matter to you. They are not counted in the totals above.

actions.title: What can I do?
actions.rights: Read about your rights under the DPDP Act

confirmed_conflict: Read both quotes in “See why”. Check whether the policy or the data-safety section is the newer one.
Ask the developer to clarify. Developers can respond through the dispute form on the About page.
potential_conflict: Read the “Why this might be fine” notes before drawing a conclusion.
If it matters to you, ask the developer which statement is current.
needs_review: Nothing is inconsistent between the sources here. Decide whether this access matters to you, and change the permission if it does.
inconclusive: Nothing can be said either way. Treat this area as unchecked, not as fine.
no_issue_detected: Nothing inconsistent turned up in the evidence we had. That is not a clearance: see what we could not check.

location: Open Android Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions → Location and choose “Allow only while using the app” or “Don't allow”.
Look for a location setting inside the app itself.
contacts: Open Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions → Contacts and choose “Don't allow” if you do not need contact features.
photos_files: In Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions, give Photos and videos or Files only the access you need (selected photos only, where offered).
camera_mic: In Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions, set Camera and Microphone to “Allow only while using the app” or “Don't allow”.
On Android 12 and later, an indicator appears in the status bar while the camera or microphone is in use.
messages_calls: In Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions, review SMS, Phone and Call logs.
Grant these only when the app clearly needs them, for example to read a one-time code.
money_payments: Check which payment methods and UPI IDs are saved in the app and remove the ones you do not use.
Look through your bank or UPI statements for anything you do not recognise.
identity: Share identity documents only when the service needs them, and ask how long the app keeps them.
You can ask the developer to correct or delete the identity details they hold.
health: In Settings → Apps → this app → Permissions, review the Health and Body sensors permissions.
Ask the developer which health data is kept and who it is shared with.
ads_tracking: Open Settings → Privacy → Ads and choose “Delete advertising ID”, or reset it.
Look for an ads or analytics opt-out inside the app.
account_profile: Look in the app under Settings or Profile for “Delete account”.
If you cannot find it, write to the grievance contact named in the policy and ask for deletion.
